Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents

Yuchen Lu Affiliation:  University of California San Diegoyuchlu17@gmail.com  jmaculey@ucsd.edu  lez023@ucsd.edu    Julian McAuley Affiliation:  University of California San Diegoyuchlu17@gmail.com  jmaculey@ucsd.edu  lez023@ucsd.edu    Lei Zhang ††thanks: Corresponding Author. Affiliation:  University of California San Diegoyuchlu17@gmail.com  jmaculey@ucsd.edu  lez023@ucsd.edu
Abstract

Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon.

1 Introduction

Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in two places: persistent task state, which embodies what has been achieved, and interaction history, which records how it was achieved (Yi et al., 2026). As shown in Figure 1, once images have been inserted into a presentation or measurements have been entered into a report, the resulting task state already captures that progress for later steps to inspect and modify (Yang et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026). As execution continues, this redundancy grows: agents repeatedly process accounts of how results already available in the task state were produced. Existing methods manage growing histories by summarizing, retrieving, or pruning past interactions (Wu et al., 2026b; Packer et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Kang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025), or by translating them into explicit progress records and structured task states (Wu et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2024). These approaches reduce context growth, but when they substitute for reusable task results, they make continuation depend on a redundant, selective account that can drift from the state the agent directly inspects and modifies.

We challenge this reliance on reconstructed accounts of progress with an object-oriented view of long-horizon context, in which reusable task objects form the basis for continuation. These objects include work products, source-grounded findings, and application states that remain usable under explicit conditions. The agent can recover relevant information through direct inspection and use of these objects, while context supplies the complementary information needed to continue. To realize this view, we introduce CarryOn, a context runtime that organizes the agent’s context into three complementary components: continuation carriers, which bind reusable content or object references to their conditions of use; execution context, which preserves active goals, applicable constraints, and unresolved issues not captured by the carriers; and live tail, which retains interactions since the most recent successful fold.

A central challenge in building object-oriented long-horizon context is retiring interaction history once progress becomes reusable without losing the information required for continuation, which poses three challenges: 1) how to identify reusable progress beyond its surrounding history: Some results still depend on prior interactions for interpretation or use. CarryOn captures these dependencies as conditions of use explicit in continuation carriers. 2) how to maintain reusable progress as the task evolves: Retaining a record does not by itself establish that its content remains supported or its referenced state remains available. CarryOn binds updates to supporting sources and applicable environment checks; across folds, affected records are revised while unaffected records are carried forward. Finally, what must remain explicit when the corresponding history is retired: Task objects do not need to capture the goals, constraints, and unresolved issues that guide subsequent execution. CarryOn jointly updates continuation carriers and execution context to preserve this complementary information, while keeping recent interactions in a live tail. Once validated, these updates are committed through a fold, replacing the covered interaction history with the resulting object-oriented context view. In this way, CarryOn progressively reorganizes the long-horizon context around reusable task objects while preserving the information required for the agent to continue.

In our experiments, object-oriented context management improves task performance while substantially reducing context cost. Our method, CarryOn, lifts Claude Opus 4.7 from 43.9% to 49.7% (+5.8%) on OSWorld 2.0 for long-horizon computer use and from 49% to 56% (+7%) on BrowseComp-Plus for long-horizon browsing. At the same time, it reduces total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, and total cost by 35.9% and 7.1%, on the two benchmarks, respectively. Compressing history alone is insufficient for continued execution: organizing context around reusable progress improves over generic compression, while the full CarryOn runtime further improves over the same principles implemented through repeated summarization. Continuation carriers and execution context play complementary roles, and reusable progress is typically maintained across folds rather than repeatedly reconstructed.

2 Related Work

Context Compression and Selection.

Existing methods reduce long-horizon context by compressing, pruning, summarizing, or selectively retrieving prior interactions (Wei et al., 2026). Compression and pruning range from prompt-level compression (Jiang et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024) to removal of redundant or outdated interactions (Xiao et al., 2026). Summarization methods periodically replace accumulated interactions with compact reasoning states or learned summaries (Wu et al., 2026b; Kang et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025), while branch-based execution can return only compact subtask results (Sun et al., 2025). External-history methods instead keep the active context bounded while preserving access to earlier interactions outside the prompt (Packer et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026), and some systems validate compressed representations against subsequent execution to reduce information loss (Chen et al., 2026b).

State Externalization and Context Reconstruction.

Complementary approaches represent task progress explicitly, reducing reliance on raw interaction history alone. Some maintain an internal state by integrating prior memory with new observations (Zhou et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025), while others use structured representations, such as execution-state trees, persistent variables, or task records (Chen et al., 2026a; Tian et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026a; Ma et al., 2026). Recent systems further externalize state into persistent workspaces and reconstruct the model’s working context through snapshots or programmatic selection (Yu et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026). Across these approaches, continuation is primarily organized around compressed interaction history or externally maintained state. Our approach instead makes reusable task objects the primary unit of continuation.

3 Method

3.1 Framework

Figure 2 illustrates CarryOn, which organizes long-horizon continuation around reusable task objects rather than the interactions that produced them. Reusable objects carry established progress for subsequent inspection and use, while explicit context retains complementary continuation information. Alongside the agent’s interaction loop, a Tracker identifies candidate reusable progress, which is bound to supporting evidence and, when applicable, checked by a Grounder. A Compiler jointly updates continuation carriers and execution context. After validation, the update replaces the covered interaction history through a fold, while subsequent interactions form a new live tail.

3.2 Context View

We organize the agent’s active context into three complementary components: continuation carriers, which expose reusable task objects; execution context, which preserves continuation information not captured by those carriers; and a live tail, which retains interactions accumulated since the latest fold.

Continuation Carriers.

Continuation carriers expose reusable progress to subsequent execution. Each carrier has a stable identity and records the reusable content or its location, together with conditions for reuse. Revisions create successor versions under the same identity, while unaffected carriers retain their records. Depending on where the reusable progress resides, CarryOn supports three forms of carriers:

  • •

    External Objects: External objects are work products that exist independently in the environment and can be reopened or modified, such as code files, documents, and spreadsheets. Their carrier records reference the underlying objects and describe the progress they capture together with conditions for reuse.

  • •

    Information Products: Information products capture reusable findings obtained through interaction, such as synthesized information or troubleshooting conclusions. When not materialized as persistent objects, the carriers store the findings directly, with supporting sources and reuse conditions.

  • •

    Situated State: Situated state captures progress available only within a particular application, session, or workflow. Reusing such progress requires returning to the environment in which the state resides. Its carrier therefore records the environment anchor, the established state, and the scope within which that state remains reusable.

These carrier types are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. A task may therefore involve multiple carriers, and the same carrier may be revised as its underlying progress evolves.

Execution Context.

Execution context complements continuation carriers by retaining information needed for execution but not encoded in reusable task objects. It records the current focus, unresolved constraints and obligations, and pending work not materialized into a reusable carrier.

Live Tail. Live tail contains the original agent–environment interactions accumulated since the most recent fold. These interactions remain directly available until incorporated into a subsequent fold.

At interaction step tt, let kk denote the most recent fold and bkb_{k} the last interaction step covered by that fold. The fold establishes a maintained set of continuation carrier records AkA_{k} and execution context EkE_{k}, while interactions occurring afterward remain in the live tail Lt=(hbk+1,…,ht)L_{t}=(h_{b_{k}+1},\ldots,h_{t}). The context view is therefore

Vt=(Ak,Ek,Lt).V_{t}=(A_{k},E_{k},L_{t}). (1)

Here, AkA_{k} exposes reusable task progress, EkE_{k} preserves complementary information needed for continuation, and LtL_{t} retains interactions not yet folded. This view provides the basis for continuation: as execution proceeds, new interactions accumulate in the live tail, while subsequent folds update the maintained carriers and execution context without reconstructing previously established progress from scratch.

3.3 Constructing and Updating the Context View

To maintain this context view during execution, CarryOn periodically folds accumulated interactions in the live tail into the maintained representation. Each fold identifies reusable progress, associates it with supporting evidence, and preserves the information still needed for continuation. The update proceeds in four stages: tracking candidates, preparing evidence, joint compilation, and validation and commitment.

Tracking Candidates.

CarryOn first identifies progress that may become reusable in subsequent execution. The Tracker maintains candidates, each representing a potential new carrier or an update to an existing one. As execution proceeds, candidates may remain under development across multiple Tracker invocations; once a candidate has reached a state that can support continuation, the Tracker requests its compilation.

A compilation request specifies both what should be compiled and the evidence needed to support it. For external objects and situated state, this includes the relevant environment object together with the state or conditions required for its reuse. For information products, it includes the source material from which reusable information should be retained. Candidates that are not yet ready remain tracked for later folds.

Preparing Evidence.

Before compilation, CarryOn first gathers the evidence authorized for each selected candidate. When compilation updates an existing carrier, it also includes the carrier’s current record. For information products, CarryOn checks that the selected material is consistent with its recorded sources. For external objects and situated state, it binds the request to the corresponding environment object, and the Grounder performs read-only checks of relevant conditions where available. The resulting input package UtU_{t} contains the selected candidates, applicable carrier records, authorized source material, object references, and available check results. This package fixes the record versions and evidence against which proposed carrier edits are later validated. Additional details are given in Appendix A.2.

Joint Compilation.

CarryOn jointly updates continuation carriers and execution context to preserve the information needed for subsequent execution. These updates are coupled: progress captured by carriers need not be duplicated in execution context, while unresolved goals, constraints, and unfinished work must remain explicit after a fold.

The Compiler receives the prepared input package UtU_{t}, containing the selected candidates, relevant prior carrier records and supporting evidence, together with the current execution context EkE_{k} and a chronological text projection Π⁡(Lt)\Pi(L_{t}) of the live tail. It proposes carrier edits Δ​At\Delta A_{t} and a revised execution context E^k+1\widehat{E}_{k+1}:

(Δ​At,E^k+1)=Compile⁡(Ut,Ek,Π⁡(Lt)).(\Delta A_{t},\widehat{E}_{k+1})=\operatorname{Compile}(U_{t},E_{k},\Pi(L_{t})). (2)

The Compiler proposes edits only for the selected candidates, grounding each edit in its authorized evidence. In contrast, the execution context is revised against the entire live tail to preserve continuation-relevant information. For external objects and situated state, the Compiler records reusable progress and its condition of use, while the underlying objects or states remain in the environment. For information products, it stores reusable findings directly in carrier records. In parallel, the Compiler revises execution context using the live tail, retaining active requirements and unfinished work not captured by carriers, including information outside the selected candidates. Upon successful validation, affected carriers receive successor versions, while unaffected carriers retain their existing records.

Validation and Commitment.

Before a proposed update changes the active context, CarryOn checks that its carrier edits still refer to the current candidate and carrier versions and are consistent with the evidence authorized for their compilation requests. It also verifies the required identity, reference, and output constraints. A successful fold must introduce at least one carrier change; revising the execution context alone does not retire interaction history. These checks guard the runtime against inconsistent or unsupported updates; they do not verify task correctness.

If these checks fail, the existing context view and live tail remain unchanged. Otherwise, CarryOn atomically applies the carrier edits and commits the revised execution context, advancing the fold through the covered interactions. In the current implementation, a successful fold covers the entire live tail. The resulting carrier set and execution context define the folded portion of the next context view, while subsequent interactions begin a new live tail.

4 Experiment

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmark.

We evaluate CarryOn on OSWorld 2.0 (Yuan et al., 2026) and BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025) to assess its performance across different types of long-horizon tasks. We use the full OSWorld 2.0 benchmark as our primary evaluation for its long execution horizons, complex workflows, and task diversity. We additionally evaluate our method on a randomly sampled subset of 100 BrowseComp-Plus questions, which require iterative search across multiple sources and provide a complementary setting for studying context management over long search histories. Benchmark details are provided in Appendix B.1.

Implementation.

We use Claude Opus 4.7 for the host agent, CarryOn’s Tracker, and Compiler. We use a 500-step budget per task on OSWorld 2.0, and the agent retrieves documents using BM25 (Robertson et al., 1995) on BrowseComp-Plus. Detailed experimental configurations and implementation settings are provided in Appendix A.3.

Evaluation Metrics.

On OSWorld 2.0, we report partial score and binary score, following the official evaluation protocol. On BrowseComp-Plus, we report answer accuracy, with final responses assessed by Qwen3-32B using the benchmark’s official grading prompt. We measure efficiency through token usage per task and cost per task, including both agent and context-management calls.

4.2 Main Result

As shown in Table 1, CarryOn boosts the partial score from 43.9% to 49.7% and binary score from 15.7% to 19.4%, exceeding other frontier models. At the same time, CarryOn reduces total token usage by 51.9% and cost per task by 35.9% as demonstrated in Table 2. These results show that CarryOn reduces long-horizon execution cost without sacrificing task performance.

We further evaluate CarryOn on a random 100-question subset of BrowseComp-Plus. CarryOn raises accuracy from 49.0% to 56.0% over the Claude Opus 4.7 baseline, while the score is also above other frontier models shown in Table 3. At the same time, total token usage decreases by 22.9% and total cost by 7.1%. Together with the OSWorld results, this shows a consistent pattern across computer-use and information-seeking tasks: CarryOn reduces context-processing overhead while maintaining or improving observed task performance.

4.3 Context and Cost Dynamics

We analyze how CarryOn’s input context and cumulative cost evolve over the course of long-horizon execution on OSWorld 2.0. As shown in Figure 3(a), the baseline context grows steadily with trajectory length, eventually exceeding 200K tokens, whereas CarryOn’s mean input context stabilizes at approximately 65K tokens after the initial growth phase. This indicates that our method maintains a consistently compact context for the agent, regardless of how long execution continues.

The corresponding cost dynamics are shown in Figure 3(b). CarryOn initially incurs additional cost from context-management calls, but this overhead is offset as repeated agent calls operate on a smaller context. The cumulative-cost curves cross before turn 200, after which the gap continues to widen; by turn 500, CarryOn reduces cumulative cost by 34.1%, including context-management overhead. Thus, the savings arise progressively as longer trajectories avoid repeatedly processing an ever-growing interaction history.

4.4 Comparison with Context Management Strategies

We examine the proposed object-oriented organization against conventional history compression, and compare the full CarryOn runtime with a summary-based implementation of the same principles. On the same random 40-task subset of OSWorld 2.0, we compare: (i) Baseline, the default OSWorld 2.0 agent setting without additional context compression; (ii) Sliding Window, which retains only recent messages; (iii) Generic Summary (GS), which summarizes earlier history into a continuation note; and (iv) CarryOn-Guided Summary (CGS), which applies our object-oriented organizing principles within a textual summary. Sliding Window and GS follow the FIFO truncation and prompting-based summarization baselines of Kang et al. (2026). All methods use the same host model (Claude Opus 4.7), the same trigger condition, and the same step budget.

As shown in Table 4, aggressive history compression does not improve performance by itself: Sliding Window and GS retain the shortest contexts but reduce both binary and partial scores relative to the baseline. Applying the same organizing principles through CGS recovers much of this loss, reaching a 50.93% partial score. Full CarryOn further increases the partial score to 55.93% while matching the baseline binary score of 22.50%. Compared with CGS, CarryOn achieves 5.00% higher partial score with about 10% shorter post-fold text. Together, these results show that our object-oriented organization principle is effective even when applied within a textual summary, while the full CarryOn runtime yields further improvements, demonstrating the additional benefit of maintaining and managing this structured state explicitly during execution.

4.5 Analysis

Carriers and the execution context are complementary.

We conduct an ablation study on the shared 40-task OSWorld 2.0 subset by hiding either continuation carriers or execution context from the host agent. As shown in Table 5, removing execution context reduces binary score from 22.50% to 17.50% and partial score from 55.93% to 44.00%, while the number of agent calls changes little. The carriers still expose completed progress, but the agent loses complementary goals, constraints, and unresolved requirements needed to finish the task. Removing continuation carriers reduces partial score to 44.62%, while increasing agent calls by 23.8% and cost by 22.3%. Without direct access to established progress, the agent must recover or reproduce earlier results before continuing. This behavior is visible in trajectory-level examples in Appendix C.2. Together, the two ablations show that carriers and execution context preserve distinct, complementary information for continuation.

Continuation carriers preserve and update progress across folds.

To examine how carrier records evolve as execution progresses, we compare them before and after each committed fold in CarryOn’s OSWorld 2.0 trajectories. Figure 4(a) shows that 80% of carrier records are retained or updated. This pattern reflects an evolving representation of task progress in which existing records remain available across folds, while updates incorporate subsequent work on the same task objects. CGS follows the same organizing principles but maintains this information by generating a complete replacement summary at each fold. Despite retaining more post-fold text, CGS achieves a lower partial score than CarryOn (50.93% vs. 55.93%) as shown in Table 4. Explicitly maintaining records as task objects evolve may help the agent build on prior progress, providing one possible explanation for CarryOn’s higher score.

Context views enable continuation from established task state.

We examine whether the agent can build on task progress after the interactions that produced it have been folded. Figure 4(b) illustrates two cases where the agent continues from existing task state, submitting a populated form and using previously saved exchange rates without repeating the corresponding work. Consistently, hiding continuation carriers increases agent calls by 23.8% as shown in Table 5, suggesting that access to established progress helps avoid redundant recovery work.

5 Conclusion

We introduce CarryOn, a context runtime that organizes long-horizon agent context around reusable task objects. Our method combines continuation carriers that expose reusable progress, execution context that preserves complementary goals, constraints, and unresolved issues, and a live tail of recent interactions. As the task progresses, CarryOn jointly updates continuation carriers and execution context to reflect evolving task state and remaining requirements, progressively replacing covered interaction history with an updated context view. On OSWorld 2.0, CarryOn raises partial score from 43.9% to 49.7% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and nominal model cost by 35.9%, including runtime overhead. On BrowseComp-Plus, it increases accuracy from 49% to 56% with lower token usage and cost. Together, these results support object-oriented context management for long-horizon agents, where task objects carry established progress and explicit context evolves with what is still needed to move forward.

Appendix A Method and Implementation Details

A.1 Context Representation and Update Procedure

CarryOn maintains an append-only interaction log, a candidate registry, versioned carrier records, and execution-context revisions. The committed carrier records and execution context define the folded portion of the context view; subsequent interactions form the live tail.

Candidate Records.

Each candidate has a runtime-assigned identifier, a provisional carrier type, a short description, and references to the interactions supporting it. Its identity fields specify the associated object or subject, and it may refer to an existing carrier whose progress is being updated. The registry records when the candidate was first observed and last revised. Candidates can persist across Tracker invocations, allowing progress to accumulate before compilation. Registering or revising a candidate does not itself trigger a fold.

Carrier Records and Versions.

A committed carrier record contains its identity, carrier type, reusable content or object reference, conditions for continuation, applicability scope, provenance, and version information. External-object identities are derived from their normalized locations. Information-product identities combine a representation type with a structured subject, while situated-state identities combine a state domain with the subject of an environment anchor. These identity fields distinguish the object being tracked from its changing contents.

Updating an existing carrier creates a successor record linked to the previous version. The successor becomes current, while earlier versions remain stored for provenance. Carriers not changed by a fold retain their current records. For information products, reusable content is stored as claims with identifiers, propositions, optional values, and supporting source references. Revisions can add, modify, or retract claims while carrying forward unaffected claims.

Execution Context.

Execution context is stored as a revision associated with a committed fold. It contains the current focus, continuity information needed to resume work, open obligations, active constraints, and immediate continuation instructions. Entries retain source attribution. The Compiler revises this information against the proposed carrier updates, preserving unresolved requirements and removing items that have been resolved or are now represented by carriers.

Update Procedure.

At each invocation, the runtime performs the following operations:

  1. 1.

    The Tracker reads recent interactions and the candidate registry. The runtime applies admissible candidate updates and resolves any compilation requests to their candidate records.

  2. 2.

    For each admitted request, the runtime binds the candidate snapshot, authorized prior carrier records, and supporting sources. Applicable environment checks contribute additional evidence. The resulting package fixes the records and evidence used for compilation. If no request is admitted, the invocation ends without a fold.

  3. 3.

    The Compiler proposes carrier additions or revisions together with a new execution context. Its input also includes the current execution context and a chronological text projection of the live tail, so continuation information outside the selected candidates can be retained.

  4. 4.

    The runtime checks identity and reference consistency, source authorization, output constraints, and whether the compilation input records remain current. A valid proposal must contain an actual carrier change. Acceptance atomically commits the carrier updates and execution-context revision and advances the fold boundary through the entire live tail. Rejection leaves these committed components and the live tail unchanged.

Previously accepted candidate updates remain available after a rejected compilation proposal. The original interactions remain in the log after a successful fold. Grounder rules and installation of the committed view are described in Appendices A.2 and A.3, respectively.

A.2 Grounder Checks and Verdict Rules

CarryOn aligns compilation requests with their supporting evidence. Information products undergo source-reference and excerpt checks. For object-bound requests, the Grounder performs scoped, read-only environment checks. Table 6 summarizes the implemented checks in the OSWorld 2.0 integration.

Request binding and evidence records.

Each check is bound to a candidate identity and revision, an object reference, a predicate, and an expected value before execution. The runtime records the observation and its provenance, and validates the binding against the current candidate before using the result.

Verdicts and compilation.

A condition is supported when the observation establishes the expected value, contradicted when it establishes an incompatible value, and unknown when the evidence cannot decide. A request is supported only when all declared conditions are supported. Any contradiction makes it contradicted. Otherwise, an unresolved condition makes it unknown.

Supported object-bound requests may proceed to compilation. Unsupported checks or unknown results leave the affected candidate uncompiled, while other admissible requests may proceed. If the interaction evidence supports an independently reusable information product, the Tracker may register a separate candidate through the source-validation route.

These checks serve as supporting consistency safeguards within the runtime, helping the agent identify explicit contradictions and outstanding task requirements.

A.3 Agent Integration and CarryOn Settings

Agent integration.

CarryOn runs alongside the agent through a benchmark-specific adapter. The adapter records interactions, supplies their textual representations and exposed thinking summaries to the runtime, and installs committed carrier records and execution context before the next agent call. Within each benchmark, the baseline and CarryOn use the same agent model, environment-action interface, and task budget. CarryOn additionally supplies the context-management interfaces and feedback described below.

Model configuration.

We use Claude Opus 4.7 for the agent, Tracker, and Compiler, without additional training. Table 7 lists their output limits and execution budgets. On OSWorld 2.0, the agent uses adaptive thinking at maximum effort; Tracker and Compiler requests contain no explicit thinking or effort override. On BrowseComp-Plus, the agent uses adaptive thinking with the provider’s default effort, the Tracker uses adaptive thinking at high effort, and the Compiler has thinking disabled. Both adapters expose the provider’s summarized thinking output to the runtime, marking it as agent-generated information rather than environment observations.

Runtime triggering.

On OSWorld 2.0, the Tracker is normally invoked when interaction text accumulated since the previous scan or fold exceeds an estimated 6,000 tokens. This estimate is the character count of the runtime’s text projection divided by four and excludes the agent’s thinking summaries. These thresholds measure text volume, not predicted monetary savings.

On BrowseComp-Plus, scan scheduling uses growth in the agent’s recorded prompt size, including cached input. The initial trigger requires 120,000 tokens of growth plus a 1,024-token margin and newly ingested search results. Consecutive scans that produce no fold double the token thresholds, up to six doublings; a successful fold resets this backoff.

OSWorld integration.

The adapter preserves the initial task message and installs a serialized checkpoint containing carrier records and execution context. It retains the contiguous suffix of complete message groups needed to preserve screenshots kept by the agent’s native image filter, together with the pending assistant message needed for protocol continuity. The native filter is configured with a recent-image threshold of 10, and screenshot eviction remains under its control. Retained tool calls, results, and signed thinking blocks preserve their protocol relationships. A fixed system instruction identifies the checkpoint as runtime-supplied context while treating its contents as task data.

BrowseComp-Plus integration.

The agent uses BM25 search with up to five results per call and 512-token snippets, without full-document retrieval. The runtime receives bounded textual projections of search results, including document identifiers, ranks, scores, and the first 160 characters of each snippet, alongside agent text and exposed thinking summaries. After a fold, pending search results remain available to the next agent call.

Installation and recovery.

Before installing a new context, the adapter snapshots the agent’s message state. A failed installation restores this snapshot and the previous active-checkpoint bookkeeping. If restoration is verified, execution continues with further runtime intervention disabled. If the previous state cannot be verified, the run stops with an error. This separates commitment of a runtime representation from its successful installation in the agent’s context.

Appendix B Experimental Details

B.1 Benchmark and Task Selection

OSWorld 2.0.

OSWorld 2.0 contains long-horizon tasks spanning seven professional domains and 21 subcategories (Yuan et al., 2026). Its workflows combine desktop applications and web services, requiring cross-source reasoning, state tracking, and coordinated operations on multiple task outputs. The benchmark reports a median estimated human completion time of approximately 1.6 hours. The duration and diversity of these workflows make it suitable for evaluating context management over extended task execution. We use the v2026.08.08 release.

Our main OSWorld 2.0 evaluation covers the full evaluation set, with both the baseline agent and CarryOn independently run by us. For the additional context-management comparisons and ablation experiments, we sample a shared subset of 40 tasks, with the following task IDs:

001, 002, 003, 004, 005, 006, 008, 009, 012, 013, 014, 018, 030, 031, 038, 039, 040, 046, 047, 048, 049, 057, 059, 061, 063, 064, 066, 070, 071, 073, 076, 079, 082, 083, 087, 089, 093, 094, 095, 102.

BrowseComp-Plus.

BrowseComp-Plus contains 830 challenging questions over a fixed corpus of 100,195 documents (Chen et al., 2025). Its questions require iterative search and reasoning across multiple sources, producing growing histories of retrieved evidence and intermediate analysis. This setting allows us to evaluate context management under sustained information accumulation. We use BM25 retrieval and evaluate both the baseline and CarryOn on the same 100-question subset, with the following question IDs:

11, 12, 15, 18, 36, 39, 209, 223, 228, 231, 233, 237, 240, 241, 246, 249, 251, 255, 256, 264, 266, 268, 480, 484, 485, 487, 495, 496, 500, 501, 502, 505, 509, 513, 515, 517, 519, 527, 528, 529, 530, 537, 544, 546, 549, 553, 555, 562, 770, 771, 773, 774, 776, 784, 787, 793, 796, 798, 801, 802, 805, 809, 819, 820, 821, 822, 827, 828, 833, 844, 850, 852, 856, 863, 869, 872, 873, 986, 991, 998, 1005, 1015, 1016, 1020, 1023, 1025, 1029, 1030, 1033, 1036, 1037, 1038, 1039, 1040, 1042, 1046, 1049, 1060, 1063, 1066.

B.2 Previously Reported Results

OSWorld 2.0.

We include the published 500-step results from the original OSWorld 2.0 evaluation (Yuan et al., 2026), retaining its reported scores and estimated model cost per task. All models receive screenshot observations through the benchmark’s official agent implementations. Claude models use their native computer-use interface, whereas all other models generate PyAutoGUI actions. GPT-5.5 executes actions in batches, while the reported Claude, MiniMax, Kimi, and Qwen results use the same single-action setting as our evaluation.

BrowseComp-Plus.

We compute external reference results on the same 100 questions used in our experiments. For GPT-5 and o3, we use the benchmark authors’ publicly released BM25 runs (Chen et al., 2025) and grade their available final responses with Qwen3-32B using the benchmark’s official grading prompt. For GPT-OSS-120B(OpenAI et al., 2025), we use the BM25(Robertson et al., 1994) configuration as the sparse retriever.

B.3 Evaluation and Resource Accounting

Accounting scope.

We report resource usage as per-task averages. For each selected task attempt, we accumulate recorded usage from both the agent and auxiliary context-management calls. For CarryOn, the latter includes the Tracker and Compiler. For summarization-based methods, it includes summarizer calls. We report agent usage, auxiliary usage, and their combined totals, so the total captures the resources consumed by both task execution and context management.

Token accounting.

Token counts come from API usage records. For task ii, let 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} contain its recorded agent and context-management calls. Total token usage is

Ti=∑j∈𝒞i(Ij+Rj+Wj+Oj),T_{i}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\left(I_{j}+R_{j}+W_{j}+O_{j}\right),

where IjI_{j} denotes uncached input tokens, RjR_{j} cache-read tokens, WjW_{j} cache-write tokens, and OjO_{j} output tokens. Cache writes include both five-minute and one-hour entries. When usage records provide an overall cache-write count and its lifetime breakdown, the breakdown partitions that count and is not added again. Reasoning tokens already included in output usage are also counted once.

Token usage is cumulative across requests: input processed again in a later call is counted again, including input served from the cache. This measures the total tokens processed during execution. We report token usage in millions, with 1​M=1061\,\mathrm{M}=10^{6} tokens.

Cost accounting.

For our Claude Opus 4.7 runs, we calculate nominal API-equivalent costs using the fixed rates in Table 8. Each call’s cost is the sum of its token counts multiplied by the corresponding category rates, and task cost is the sum across calls. The same rates apply to the agent and CarryOn’s auxiliary models.

Cached input remains part of total token usage but receives its corresponding cache price. Consequently, reductions in token usage and cost can differ depending on the proportions of uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output. Reported totals include context-management overhead and exclude evaluator, user-simulator, and infrastructure costs. They cover the recorded usage of the selected task attempts.

Aggregation.

For each method, we average task totals over its reported task set. Relative reductions in token usage and model cost are computed from these means:

Reduction⁡(x)=100​(1−x¯CarryOnx¯baseline)%,\operatorname{Reduction}(x)=100\left(1-\frac{\bar{x}_{\mathrm{CarryOn}}}{\bar{x}_{\mathrm{baseline}}}\right)\%,

where x¯\bar{x} is mean token usage or model cost per task. All calculations use unrounded values, with rounding applied only to the displayed results.

Appendix C Supplementary Results and Analysis

C.1 Statistical Procedures for Context and Carrier Analysis

Context and cost dynamics.

Figure 3 uses the per-call usage traces of all baseline and CarryOn trajectories included in the resource comparison. An agent turn denotes a metered agent-model response, including retries and terminal-review responses with recorded usage. For method mm, let Lm,iL_{m,i} denote the number of such responses in trajectory ii, and define the active set at turn tt as 𝒜m​(t)={i:Lm,i≥t}\mathcal{A}_{m}(t)=\{i:L_{m,i}\geq t\}. We compute

P¯m​(t)=1|𝒜m​(t)|​∑i∈𝒜m​(t)Pm,i,t,C¯m​(t)=1|𝒜m​(t)|​∑i∈𝒜m​(t)Cm,i​(t).\bar{P}_{m}(t)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_{m}(t)|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{m}(t)}P_{m,i,t},\qquad\bar{C}_{m}(t)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_{m}(t)|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{m}(t)}C_{m,i}(t).

Here, Pm,i,tP_{m,i,t} is the input token count reported by the API, including uncached input, cache reads, and cache creation. Screenshot tokens remain included. Cm,i​(t)C_{m,i}(t) accumulates agent costs through turn tt and runtime costs assigned to the same boundary, using the accounting rules in Appendix B.3. Gray bars show the fraction of baseline trajectories that remain active at each turn, sampled every ten turns.

Curve smoothing and annotations.

We first compute the per-turn means and then apply a Gaussian filter with a standard deviation of 12 turns, a kernel truncated at four standard deviations, and symmetric reflection at the boundaries. Input-context curves use the complete recorded series before the displayed range is restricted to 500 turns. Cost curves are smoothed over turns 0–500, with the unsmoothed series initialized at zero cumulative cost. Gray bars are also smoothed for visualization. Figure annotations are calculated from the raw data. Shading shows the difference between the two cost curves.

Post-fold text length.

For Table 4, we measure the textual context immediately after each installed fold, before the next observation is appended. All methods use the same text projection, including task instructions, retained records or summaries, interaction text, returned thinking summaries, and role/action/observation labels. Image data, signatures, fixed system prompts, and tool schemas are excluded. Length is measured in thousands of Unicode characters. We first average lengths across folds within each task and then average equally across tasks with at least one fold. The baseline has no post-fold measurement. We use this measure together with task performance to compare how much text each method retains and how well the agent performs.

Carrier persistence across folds.

For Figure 4(a), we compare current carrier records before and after each committed and installed fold. We examine all 494 committed and installed folds across the CarryOn trajectories included in this analysis. Carrier identities are tracked across record versions using registered identities and successor relations. A carrier is retained when its current record version is unchanged, updated when a successor version is committed, and added when it has no predecessor. Each carrier contributes one observation per fold in which it is present afterward. The same carrier can therefore contribute across several folds, and initial creations are included. Pooling these observations gives 278 retained, 372 updated, and 163 added observations, for 813 in total. The retained-or-updated proportion is 650/813≈79.95%650/813\approx 79.95\%, rounded to 80%80\% in the figure. These percentages describe record continuity across folds.

C.2 Continuation Cases and Ablation Behaviors

We inspect recorded trajectories to show how execution continues after a fold and how the agent behaves when carrier records are hidden. The tables present selected steps, the information retained at the fold, and subsequent actions.

Continuing from established progress.

Table 9 shows a publication form that remains populated across a fold. The agent checks the existing entries and submits the form without re-entering the authors. The saved screenshot confirms submission, and the paper subsequently appears in the Research Output list.

Returning to previously acquired information.

Table 10 compares two runs of a prize-distribution task. In the full CarryOn run, the agent continues filling the form after the fold. In the carrier-masking run, it has already established the item-price mapping and used it to construct a plan. After the fold, it questions whether the prices have been confirmed, extracts the PDF again, and reopens the catalogue to reconstruct the mapping. This provides a concrete example of repeated information acquisition when carrier records are withheld.

Appendix D Prompts

The Tracker and Compiler use separate system prompts. The runtime selects an environment, information-product, or composite Compiler route according to the authorized candidates. For presentation, prompt terminology is standardized to match the paper: continuation carriers (carriers for short), the host agent, and the runtime scheduler. An environment-check specification lists conditions for the Grounder to check; selected evidence forms part of the compilation input package UtU_{t}. Internal policy labels, development annotations, and serialization-version tags are omitted. JSON field names and categorical values retain their implementation spelling.

Runtime inputs.

The Tracker receives the task and current committed records, the live tail, and a current-state block containing candidates and runtime feedback. The Compiler additionally receives the authorized compilation requests and their source bindings. These blocks are populated for each invocation.

Summary inputs.

GS and CGS receive the current visible conversation, including the task, any earlier summary, and recent messages. The input preserves message roles, tool actions, returned observations, visible images, and returned reasoning summaries where available. They return a replacement summary as plain text.
